To meet the G/NG Milestone 2.5.4: Recover >90 wt% of two different commercial rigid films and demonstrate that recovered resins have properties similar to pure resins, computational and experimental efforts optimized polymer drying conditions to reduce the solvent retained within the recovered polymers; solvent retention was found to impact melt flow rheology (MFR) measurements. Final drying conditions led to >90 wt% polymer recoveries and MFR measurements within 25% of benchmarks for the PE and PET components of two rigid films provided by Amcor, thus meeting Milestone 2.5.4. Figure 3.5.1 shows an example process flow diagram and experimental recoveries for one of the two rigid films which has 5 total polymer components. Figure 3.5.1: Diagram illustrating the sequence of STRAP dissolution and precipitation steps to recover all five polymer components of a rigid multilayer film provided by Amcor. The film included PETG, PE, EVA, EVOH, and PET, with each removed using solvents, antisolvents (in the case of PETG), and operating temperatures suggested experimentally. Melt flow index measurements after optimizing the drying of recovered resins were within 25% of virgin materials. These results, when combined with similar data for a second rigid film, met G/NG Milestone 2.5.4. Task 3.5: Development of STRAP for rigid and flexible PIW films extended the methods in Task 2.5 to flexible PIW films. A key focus was methods to recover pure, color-free resins from printed films because the presence of residual color in recycled resins substantially reduces their value. We thus sought to develop new computational and experimental methods to remove inks and related colorants during STRAP. In addition, we sought to develop methods to create larger quantities of STRAP resins (~kg) in order to cast films using industrial equipment available at Amcor. Cast films permit analysis of mechanical properties relevant to the use of STRAP resins in film applications. Given these considerations and the success of the computational methods developed in Task 2.5, we abandoned Milestone 3.5.1: Develop machine learning models for polymer solubility, mechanical properties, and rheological behavior based on experimental results and use to update solvent design in favor of focusing on color removal and scale-up (with eventual relevance to Milestone 4.5.2 as detailed below). Using the computational and experimental methods developed in Task 2.5, we designed STRAP processes for two flexible post-industrial films: a printed film containing PE, EVOH, PET, and a polyurethane binder (we refer to this as the printed film), and a clear film containing polyamide-6 (PA6), PE, and EVOH (we refer to this as the nylon film). We designed STRAP processes and characterized yields, melt temperatures, crystallinities for the recovered polymers, all of which were similar to virgin reference materials. For the printed film, we additionally scaled up production to ~1 kg using a new method that maintained high-temperature dissolution and precipitation steps using a jacketed vessel.
